title: Free as the wilderness (Numbers Rabbah 1:7)
hookLine: the Torah was given in the desert, free as fire and water, to whoever makes themselves open
tomorrow: what happens to God's name when nobody bears witness?

lines: WHO GETS IT? WHAT DOES IT COST?
cards: Some things have no paywall. A public library card. A water fountain in the park.
The sunset over a parking lot. Nobody checks your ID at a sunset. The book of Numbers opens with an address: God spoke to Moses "in the wilderness of Sinai."
Not a city. Not a palace. Not a temple with a door and a guard.
Why there? One question for today: who gets the Torah, and what does it cost?

teach.b: Numbers Rabbah answers with three things. The Torah came with fire, on a smoking mountain. With water, as clouds poured down.
And in the wilderness. All three are free to everyone in the world. So are the words of Torah: free to all who come.
Then a second line, the hard one: whoever doesn't make themselves ownerless like the wilderness can't acquire wisdom and Torah.
The Hebrew is hefker, land nobody owns. A desert has no gate, no owner, no fence. So the price isn't money.
It's openness. That may be why the line is hard: paying for something is often easier than putting down what you already guard. Now a neighbor.
In the Gospel of Matthew, when Jesus sends out his disciples, he tells them, in the King James words, "freely ye have received, freely give."
Some Christian readers hear in it a charge to share what God gave without charging for it. Shared ground: a gift from God that came free and should stay free.
The honest difference: in Matthew, the gift is what the disciples received from Jesus and are sent to pass on.

teach.h: THE GIFT, AND WHO MUST OPEN.
teach.b: In the midrash, the gift is the Torah itself, and the condition sits on the receiver: be as open as a desert.
Each says it in its own words, from its own book, and neither needs the other to be the same.

how: Jewish study is traditionally open to any learner who comes, and Jews read Numbers Rabbah's teaching about the wilderness around Shavuot, when the book of Numbers and the giving of the Torah are both in view.

games.q: what does “free as the wilderness” mean?
o: the Torah is free to all, like open desert land
the Torah belongs far from cities and crowds
the Torah was hidden away in a cave in the desert

games.q: free, and for whom — tap the pairs.
p: free to everyone in the world
freely ye have received, freely give

s: the desert in this midrash is just where the Israelites happened to be
Numbers Rabbah reads it as the lesson itself: free and owned by no one.
the midrash names three things the Torah came with, all free to everyone
Matthew and the midrash say exactly the same thing
both speak of a gift that came free; in Matthew it's what the disciples pass on, in the midrash it's the Torah, open to the open.

games.q: a new neighbor asks you a clumsy, skeptical question about a Jewish practice. by Numbers Rabbah, how do you treat it?
o: wait until they show they're serious enough to deserve a real answer.
answer openly; a question is a door opening, and the teaching is free.
tell them it's not yours to give away and they should ask a rabbi.
games.why: the Torah is free as fire, water and wilderness to all who come; the only condition is openness, and asking is a start.

practice: Close your eyes and let your hands rest loose, shoulders down. Picture open desert in every direction: no fence, no door, no owner.
For the rest of the sit, whenever you catch yourself guarding something, a grudge, an opinion, a plan, let that fence come down a little.

wordCard.voice: Free as the wilderness: Numbers Rabbah on why the Torah was given in the desert. Free to all, like fire and water, for anyone who makes themselves open.

orig.note: Hebrew: ownerless. make yourself hefker like the wilderness, says the midrash, and you can receive Torah.

carryVoice: Your line: free as the wilderness. Nobody owns a desert, and the only price is being open.

sources.ref: Numbers Rabbah 1:7 (the Torah given through fire, water and wilderness, free to all; whoever does not make himself hefker like the wilderness cannot acquire wisdom and Torah)

sources.q: freely ye have received, freely give
